You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel — Review of Seller's SPA Positions & Disclosure Letter

Jae, I've reviewed the Seller's update and Disclosure Letter against our baseline (100% of Paperbark, AUD 24m, debt-free/cash-free, NSW law). Below are the material issues, my reasoning, and recommendations. Several of these are value items (real money off price or indemnity) and a couple are deal-protection issues we should treat as non-negotiable.

---

## A. Liability architecture — Seller over-reaching

**1. Fundamental/Title warranties lumped in with general cap and time limit (CRITICAL)**
> "capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity."

This is not "administrative simplicity" — it's a substantive giveaway. If title to the shares fails, we could have paid AUD 24m and be capped at recovering AUD 4.8m, with the claim time-barred after 18 months. Title and capacity go to whether we actually got what we paid for.
- **Push back:** Title/capacity/authority warranties must be capped at **100% of purchase price (AUD 24m)** and carved out of the short limitation period (minimum 6–7 years, or the general statutory limitation period). This is market-standard and should be a red line.

**2. Tax warranties folded into the general 18-month limit**
> "The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime."

Tax exposures typically surface on audit/amendment well beyond 18 months. Tax warranties and a tax indemnity/covenant should run to **at least 7 years** (aligned to the ATO amendment period). Don't accept the general regime for tax.

**3. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"**
This default-drafting trick means any ambiguity resolves in the Seller's favour. Flip it: limitations apply **only** to general warranty claims, and expressly **do not** apply to title, tax, fundamental warranties, specific indemnities, or fraud/wilful concealment. Carve out fraud explicitly — a cap/time-bar that survives fraud is unenforceable in principle and we should never concede it.

**4. Exclusive-remedy / non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (Cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)**
A blanket exclusive-remedy + non-reliance clause attempts to shut down claims for misrepresentation and, read broadly, fraud. **Carve out fraud and fraudulent misrepresentation** (non-excludable anyway, but say so). Ensure specific indemnities (see below) are not swallowed by the exclusive-remedy clause.

**5. Cap level and basket mechanics**
- 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) is within normal range for general warranties — acceptable in principle, subject to carve-outs above.
- De minimis AUD 25k and basket AUD 250k are broadly market. Confirm the basket is a genuine "excess over basket" (tipping vs deductible); the Seller has drafted it as a **deductible** ("only the excess above the basket is recoverable"). We'd prefer a **tipping basket** (recover from dollar one once threshold crossed). Negotiable but worth pushing.

---

## B. Buyer knowledge / disclosure sandbagging — this is where the Disclosure Letter is doing heavy lifting

**6. Clause 8.3 — constructive knowledge bar (CRITICAL)**
> "no claim … of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

Combined with the Disclosure Letter's **general sweep disclosure** (para 1.1–1.2: "every fact … contained or referred to in the data room … and publicly searchable corporate records"), this is a deliberate construction to **disclose everything and nothing**. The effect: the Seller dumps the data room, deems it all disclosed, and then bars us from claiming on anything "discoverable."

This guts the warranties. Reasoning: warranties exist precisely to allocate risk of things we *didn't* find. A "deemed discoverable" bar rewards the Seller for burying problems in a data room.

- **Push back hard:**
  - Delete constructive/"discoverable" knowledge. Limit any knowledge qualifier to the **actual knowledge of named Buyer deal individuals**, if we concede it at all.
  - Reject general/sweep disclosure. Disclosure must be **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope** of the matter, and tied to **specific** warranties. A document merely sitting in the data room is not disclosure.
  - Delete the "public registers" deemed disclosure.

**7. Para 1.4 — non-admission wrapper**
Standard and acceptable *as a non-admission*, but it must not convert the specific disclosures into effective disclosure against the warranties. Fine so long as B6 fixes are made.

---

## C. Specific disclosed problems — these need indemnities or price/completion mechanics, NOT just "disclosure"

The Disclosure Letter discloses several live problems. The Seller's strategy is to disclose them (to block warranty claims) while offering no protection. Each should be converted into a **specific indemnity** (uncapped by the general cap, outside the basket) and/or a **condition to Completion**.

**8. Bluefen change-of-control consent (~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30%) (CRITICAL)**
> Seller: "reasonable endeavours … treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent." Disclosure: no final consent and no evidence conditions (cl 11.3) satisfied.

30% of revenue sits on one contract with a change-control clause. "Reasonable endeavours" is weak and the drafting lets the Seller deem the condition satisfied on bare delivery of a consent even if the 11.3 conditions aren't met.
- **Push back:** Make **actual Bluefen written consent (with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied)** a hard **condition precedent to Completion**. If we must accept post-completion, demand a **specific indemnity** for lost Bluefen revenue/termination, plus possibly a **price retention/escrow**. This is a potential walk-away item — losing 30% of revenue changes the valuation materially.

**9. Riverlark facility ~AUD 3.2m — "release following Completion" (CRITICAL — debt-free/cash-free breach)**
> Seller: release *after* Completion; Disclosure: not repaid, no discharge of security.

Our deal is **debt-free/cash-free**. AUD 3.2m of debt (with security) cannot survive Completion.
- **Push back:** Riverlark must be **repaid and security discharged at or before Completion**, funded from the price via the funds flow (we pay AUD 24m gross; AUD 3.2m goes to Riverlark). Require a **payout letter and deed of release/discharge of security as a condition to Completion**. "Release following Completion" is unacceptable — we are not taking the Company subject to a secured creditor.

**10. DD-005 closing bonuses AUD 420,000 — "a matter for the Seller … not itemised in funds flow" (value leakage)**
> Disclosure: conditional on Completion + continued employment; not in funds flow; silent on payroll tax/super/on-costs.

These bonuses are **triggered by the transaction**. If they're obligations of the Company payable post-Completion, *we* bear them — plus super (~11–12%), payroll tax, and on-costs, pushing the real cost above AUD 470k. Saying it's "a matter for the Seller" while leaving it off the funds flow is exactly how the liability lands on the Buyer.
- **Push back:** Either (a) Seller pays/discharges all transaction bonuses and on-costs at Completion, or (b) a **specific indemnity** for the full bonus amount **plus all on-costs (super, payroll tax)**, or (c) an explicit **purchase price reduction / completion accounts adjustment**. Confirm treatment of super and payroll tax expressly.

**11. Export/privacy incident DD-006 (~1,240 records) (CRITICAL — contingent liability)**
> Seller: "preliminary operational matter … not expected to be material." Disclosure: can't yet establish access, scope or notifiability; investigation preliminary.

This is a potential **eligible data breach under the Privacy Act (NDB scheme)**. 1,240 records with names/emails/roles could trigger OAIC notification obligations and individual notifications; exposure includes regulatory penalties (recently materially increased), remediation, and reputational harm. The Seller's characterisation ("not expected to be material") is self-serving and contradicted by its own disclosure that scope is unknown.
- **Push back:**
  - **Specific indemnity** covering all costs, fines, remediation, notification and third-party claims arising from the incident — **uncapped by the general cap and the basket**, and with a **longer time limit**.
  - Pre-completion covenant requiring the Seller to complete the investigation, make any required notifications, and keep us informed.
  - Specific warranty on privacy/data compliance that is **not** deemed disclosed-away by the general sweep.

**12. Ironquay IP / SOW3 (DD-004, AUD 180,000 open)**
> Seller: existing indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment … adequate." Disclosure: cl 7.3 transfers SOW3 Project Materials only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee; no proof of payment or assignment in data room.

The risk isn't just the AUD 180k — it's that **IP ownership in the SOW3 Project Materials doesn't vest** until all fees are paid, so the Company may **not own IP it relies on**. Capping the indemnity at the payment amount ignores the ownership/operational risk if materials are core.
- **Push back:** First assess whether SOW3 materials are material to the product. Require **evidence of payment and a confirmatory IP assignment** as a condition, or an indemnity covering **loss of/inability to use the IP**, not merely the fee. Reject the "adequate" framing until we see the assignment.

**13. Supplier renewals — Sandbar AUD 330k (DD-008/011)**
> Seller: "ordinary-course operating costs." Disclosure: silent on whether unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in ordinary course.

Three related AUD 110k renewals read together (note the Seller split them — query whether structured to stay under a materiality/consent threshold). If committed pre-Completion for future periods, they're liabilities we inherit.
- **Push back:** Clarify timing, term and termination rights. If they're non-ordinary-course commitments, treat as a leakage/adjustment item or require Seller discharge. At minimum, an **ordinary-course-of-business warranty** that is not disclosed-away.

**14. Office lease notification (DD-007) & Mossvale assignment restriction (DD-009)**
Seller says neither requires consent for a *share* sale. That may be right (share sale ≠ assignment), but verify the actual clauses — some leases/contracts define "change of control" as a deemed assignment or breach. Low-to-medium priority: confirm by reading the clauses, don't accept the Seller's characterisation at face value.

---

## D. Title

**15. Title evidenced "by the share register at DD-012"**
The register is evidence but not conclusive. Combined with issue #1 (title warranty capped/time-barred), our protection is thin.
- **Push back:** Full **title/capacity warranties at 100% cap, long limitation** (per B1), plus standard Completion deliverables (share certificates, executed transfers, board resolutions registering transfer, updated register). Confirm no encumbrances over the shares.

---

## Summary of Recommendations (priority order)

**Red lines / conditions to Completion:**
1. **Riverlark AUD 3.2m repaid + security discharged at Completion** — debt-free/cash-free is non-negotiable; funded from price.
2. **Bluefen actual consent (with cl 11.3 conditions met) as a CP** — 30% of revenue; fallback is specific indemnity + escrow.
3. **Title/capacity/authority warranties: 100% cap, long limitation** — carve out of general regime.
4. **Fraud carve-out** from all caps, time limits, baskets, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses.

**Delete / reverse the sandbagging:**
5. Delete **constructive/"discoverable" knowledge** (Cl 8.3) and the **general sweep disclosure** (Disclosure 1.1–1.2, public registers). Require **fair, specific disclosure** tied to specific warranties.
6. Flip the default: limitations apply **only** to general warranty claims.

**Convert disclosed problems into specific indemnities (outside cap/basket, longer time limit):**
7. **Privacy/export incident (DD-006)** — full indemnity + pre-completion remediation covenant.
8. **DD-005 bonuses AUD 420k + on-costs (super/payroll tax)** — Seller discharge, indemnity, or price adjustment; put on funds flow.
9. **Ironquay SOW3** — indemnity covering IP non-vesting (not just the fee) + confirmatory assignment/payment evidence.

**Tax & diligence tidy-ups:**
10. **Tax warranties + tax covenant to 7 years**, outside the general regime.
11. Prefer a **tipping basket**; confirm de minimis/basket mechanics.
12. Verify lease (DD-007), Mossvale (DD-009) and Sandbar renewals (DD-008/011) clauses directly — don't rely on Seller characterisations; add ordinary-course warranty.

**Overall take:** The package is Seller-friendly and leans heavily on a "disclose-everything + constructive-knowledge bar" strategy to neutralise the warranties, while pushing the Riverlark debt and transaction bonuses onto us contrary to the debt-free/cash-free basis. The biggest substantive risks are Bluefen (revenue concentration), Riverlark (secured debt), and the privacy incident (open-ended regulatory exposure). I'd frame our mark-up around the four red lines first.

---

Want me to draft a mark-up / issues list in a table for the Seller, or prepare suggested redline wording for the title cap carve-out, the fraud carve-out, and the specific indemnities? I can also calculate the grossed-up bonus/on-cost exposure if you give me the super and payroll-tax assumptions. 

*(Note: this is deal-support analysis, not a final legal opinion — specific clause wording should be confirmed against the full executed SPA text, which we only have in summary here.)*
=== END ADVICE ===
